title: The 74-Year Mystery of Australia's Somerton Man Solved

segments.narration: On December 1, 1948, a body washed up on Australia's Somerton Beach with every single clothing tag neatly cut out.
Hidden inside a secret trouser pocket was a torn paper scrap reading Tamam Shud—Persian for 'It is finished.'
Nearby, police found a book containing a cryptic, uncrackable code. Was this man an international spy who knew too much?
For 74 years, the case baffled detectives—until 2022, when advanced DNA sequencing extracted genetic data from his hair.
The mystery master spy wasn't an assassin at all, but Carl Webb, a quiet Melbourne engineer who simply walked away.

verdicts.claim: On December 1, 1948, an unidentified man's body was discovered on Somerton Beach in Australia with all clothing tags removed.
verdicts.note: The article confirms the body was found on Somerton Park beach on 1 December 1948, and all labels on his clothes had been removed.

verdicts.claim: A torn paper scrap featuring the Persian text Tamam Shud was discovered in a hidden pocket of the dead man's trousers.
verdicts.note: The article states a scrap of paper printed with the Persian phrase 'tamám shud' was found in the fob pocket of the man's trousers.

verdicts.claim: Investigators found a mysterious, uncracked code written inside a book connected to the dead man.
verdicts.note: The article confirms detectives found indentations of text resembling a coded message on the inside back cover of the connected book, which has not been deciphered.

verdicts.claim: In 2022, hair preserved from the Somerton Man was used to perform DNA sequencing and trace his family tree.
verdicts.note: The article states that in July 2022, researchers used genetic genealogy from DNA extracted from the man's hair to trace his identity.

verdicts.claim: Genetic genealogy identified the Somerton Man as Carl Webb, an electrical instrument maker from Melbourne.
verdicts.note: The article states genetic genealogy identified him as Carl 'Charles' Webb, an electrical engineer and instrument maker, though it does not explicitly specify Melbourne.
